Abstract
This article evaluates how far Tanzania’s Cybercrimes Act prevents, detects, and secures the prosecution of mobile money fraud that begins with an unsolicited message. It combines a doctrinal reading of sections 12 and 20 of the Act and its investigative provisions with empirical data collected in Dodoma through semi-structured interviews and open-ended questionnaires administered to twenty respondents from law enforcement, regulatory bodies, telecommunications companies, Parliament, academia and victims of fraud. The Act gives investigators a usable legal foundation, yet 65 per cent of respondents rated it less than effective. Section 12 is built around the manipulation of computer data or systems and fits awkwardly with schemes in which the victim is persuaded to make the transfer personally, while section 20 predates AI-generated voice calls, deepfakes, QR code scams and spoofed sender names, none of which the Act mentions. Enforcement is further weakened by thin forensic capacity, slow information sharing between agencies and service providers, and low digital literacy among users; no reported decision applying either provision to this kind of fraud could be found. The article argues that the problem is one of design as well as enforcement: an offence built around the manipulation of machines cannot be relied upon to punish the manipulation of people. It offers what appears to be the first focused legal assessment of this fraud vector in Tanzania and proposes legislative, institutional, and awareness-based reforms, including a technology-neutral offence of causing loss by electronic deception, mandatory fraud reporting by operators, a victim compensation mechanism that does not depend on conviction, stronger forensic capacity and sustained public education

ABSTRACT 
This article evaluates how far Tanzania’s Cybercrimes Act prevents, 
detects, and secures the prosecution of mobile money fraud that begins with 
an unsolicited message. It combines a doctrinal reading of sections 12 and 
20 of the Act and its investigative provisions with empirical data collected 
in Dodoma through semi-structured interviews and open-ended 
questionnaires administered to twenty respondents from law enforcement, 
regulatory bodies, telecommunications companies, Parliament, academia 
and victims of fraud. The Act gives investigators a usable legal foundation, 
yet 65 per cent of respondents rated it less than effective. Section 12 is built 
around the manipulation of computer data or systems and fits awkwardly 
with schemes in which the victim is persuaded to make the transfer 
personally, while section 20 predates AI-generated voice calls, deepfakes, 
QR code scams and spoofed sender names, none of which the Act mentions. 
Enforcement is further weakened by thin forensic capacity, slow 
information sharing between agencies and service providers, and low 
digital literacy among users; no reported decision applying either provision 
to this kind of fraud could be found. The article argues that the problem is 
one of design as well as enforcement: an offence built around the 
manipulation of machines cannot be relied upon to punish the manipulation 
of people. It offers what appears to be the first focused legal assessment of 
this fraud vector in Tanzania and proposes legislative, institutional, and 
awareness-based reforms, including a technology-neutral offence of 
causing loss by electronic deception, mandatory fraud reporting by 
operators, a victim compensation mechanism that does not depend on 
conviction, stronger forensic capacity and sustained public education.

INTRODUCTION 
Few innovations have changed everyday 
economic life in Tanzania as quickly as mobile 
money. M-Pesa, Airtel Money, Mixx by Yas 
(formerly Tigo Pesa) and HaloPesa allow people 
without bank accounts to send and receive money, 
pay bills, buy goods and save, using a basic 
handset and a dense network of agents.1 For many 
rural households, a mobile wallet is the first 
formal financial account they have held, and the 
gains for financial inclusion have been 
substantial. Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania are 
among the few countries in the world where 
mobile money accounts outnumber bank 
accounts, and the service has grown from simple 
transfers into savings, credit and even insurance 
products.2 
The features that make the service attractive, 
namely speed, reach and simplicity, have also 
made it a target. A large share of losses now 
comes not from breaking into operators’ systems, 
but from messages the user never asked for: a text 
claiming that money was sent by mistake, a call 
from someone posing as customer care, a 
WhatsApp link promising a prize or an instant 
loan. Smishing is phishing by SMS; vishing uses 
voice calls; spoofing disguises the sender’s 
number or name so that the message appears to 
come from a trusted institution.3 What unites these

schemes is that they work on the person rather

The harm is not confined to individual losses. 
Each successful scam erodes public confidence in 
digital payments, and that confidence is what 
financial inclusion rests on.5 Studies in Tanzania 
have found that users who fear fraud reduce their 
use of the service or change how they use it, which 
slows the very adoption that policy seeks to 
encourage.6 This raises a question of legal design. 
Tanzania’s principal weapon against such conduct 
is the Cybercrimes Act, but a statute written 
largely to punish interference with computers may 
not sit comfortably with fraud that depends on 
deception and on the victim’s own action. 
Whether the Act, as drafted and as applied, is 
equal to that task is the subject of this article. 
Background 
Many jurisdictions struggled to respond to online 
transaction crime because their criminal law had 
no settled definition of it and did not explain how 
it differed from ordinary fraud. The international 
answer, reflected in the Council of Europe’s 
Convention on Cybercrime, was to create a 
distinct offence of computer-related fraud defined

Parliament enacted the Cybercrimes Act in 2015, 
and it now appears as Cap 443 in the 2023 Revised 
Edition. The Act applies to both Mainland 
Tanzania and Tanzania Zanzibar and is designed 
to criminalise offences relating to computer 
systems and to provide for the investigation of 
such offences and the use of electronic evidence. 
Two provisions are central here. Section 12 
creates the offence of computer-related fraud, 
committed where a person, with fraudulent or 
dishonest intent, causes loss of property to another 
through the input, alteration, deletion, delaying or 
suppression of computer data or through 
interference with the functioning of a computer 
system. Section 20 prohibits a person, with intent 
to commit an offence under the Act, from 
initiating, relaying or retransmitting unsolicited 
messages or falsifying header information in 
them.9 The Act was preceded by the introduction 
of compulsory SIM card registration, which was 
intended to remove the anonymity on which 
telephone fraud had depended.10 
On paper these provisions seem to reach the 
conduct described above, yet fraud continues to 
grow. Part of the explanation lies in the pace of 
technological change. When the Bill was debated, 
the typical scam was a clumsily worded text 
message. Fraudsters can now imitate the voice of 
a relative or a bank officer with artificial 
intelligence, circulate deepfake videos endorsing 
bogus investment schemes, direct victims to QR 
codes that trigger payments, and make messages

The Act mentions none of these techniques, and

between a static statute and constantly shifting

burden falls on a small number of investigators 
and prosecutors who must fit new schemes within

by amending the text, by reading existing 
provisions broadly, or by strengthening the 
institutions that apply them is the underlying 
policy problem this article addresses. 
Research Question 
The study is guided by one question: how 
effective is the Cybercrimes Act in preventing, 
detecting and prosecuting mobile money fraud 
resulting from unsolicited messaging in 
Tanzania? 
Answering it requires attention to two related 
matters, namely whether the text of the Act 
reaches the conduct in question and whether the 
institutions responsible for applying it are able to 
do so in practice.14 The first is a question of 
statutory interpretation; the second is a question of 
implementation that can only be answered by 
asking those who work with the Act. 
Significance and Scope 
Scholarship on cybercrime in Tanzania has 
grown, but it tends either to treat the Cybercrimes 
Act as a whole or to approach mobile money fraud 
from a technical or commercial angle.15 Few

The scope is deliberately narrow. Although the 
Act applies throughout the United Republic, the 
study is confined to Mainland Tanzania, with 
primary data collected in Dodoma. Legally, it 
concentrates on sections 12 and 20 and the 
procedural powers that support them, read 
alongside complementary statutes on electronic 
transactions, communications, payment systems 
and data protection.16 It examines both doctrinal 
adequacy, that is, whether the text reaches the 
conduct, and practical implementation, that is, 
whether the institutions can apply it. 
LITERATURE REVIEW 
Akinbowale, Mashigo and Zerihun show that 
cyberfraud in African financial systems relies 
heavily on phishing and social engineering, and 
that users’ limited awareness matters to fraudsters 
as much as any technical weakness; they also 
stress that detection tools, internal controls and 
user education must work together. Goldbarsht 
and de Koker make a related point about 
regulation: financial technology opens new routes 
to crime that cannot be closed by technology 
alone, only by laws, compliance duties and 
enforcement that develop alongside the 
platforms.17 Tanzanian studies bring these 
observations closer to home. Salim’s study of 
telecom providers in Zanzibar identifies

Pallangyo attributes the vulnerability of mobile

On the legal side, Shelimo compares Tanzania’s

capacity; Nashon reviews the implementation of

Massawe and Mshana reach similar conclusions 
from inside the Police Force’s investigation unit, 
while Sibe and Kaunert show, from the Nigerian

decisive factor in whether financial cybercrime 
can be prosecuted at all.20 Together, these studies 
document the prevalence and mechanics of 
mobile money fraud and the general weaknesses 
of enforcement, but none of them tests whether the 
particular offences in the Cybercrimes Act are 
adequate for fraud that begins with an unsolicited 
message.

Nigeria rather than the meeting point between

platforms, while Majamba and Mwaburi are 
concerned with regional harmonisation rather 
than with the fit between particular offences and 
particular frauds.21 No study appears to have read 
sections 12 and 20 closely against the techniques 
now used to defraud mobile money users, and then 
tested that reading against the experience of those 
who investigate, prosecute, regulate and suffer 
from the fraud. This article does both. It pairs a 
doctrinal analysis of the two provisions and their 
procedural support with interview and 
questionnaire data from police investigators, 
public prosecutors, regulators, 
telecommunications officers, legislators, a legal 
scholar, an artificial intelligence expert and 
victims. To the author’s knowledge, it is the first 
focused legal assessment of this fraud vector in 
Tanzania. 
CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK 
Cybercrime 
Holt, Bossler and Seigfried-Spellar describe 
cybercrime as criminal activity committed 
through computers, networks or other digital 
devices, whether the device is the target of the 
offence or the means of committing it, and they 
observe that the most damaging cybercrimes 
increasingly exploit human trust rather than 
technical flaws.22 The category covers offences as 
different as unauthorised access, data 
interference, identity theft, online fraud and the 
unlawful interception of communications. It 
supplies the wider legal setting within which 
mobile money fraud occurs, and in Tanzania it is 
governed principally by the Cybercrimes Act, 
which groups these offences in Part II.23

Mobile Money 
Mobile money is electronically stored monetary 
value, linked to a mobile phone account and 
issued by a licensed provider, that can be used to 
transfer funds, make payments and save without a 
conventional bank account.24 The account is 
identified by the SIM card and phone number 
rather than by a bank account number, while the 
corresponding cash is held in trust in a 
commercial bank.25 Because it rides on existing 
mobile networks and agents, it reaches people 
whom banks have never served, which explains 
both its value to users and its attraction to 
fraudsters. 
Mobile Money Fraud 
Mobile money fraud means any deceptive act 
committed through a mobile money platform for 
financial gain. Its common forms include 
phishing, smishing, spoofing, SIM swap fraud and 
fake customer care calls.26 Unlike conventional 
theft, it usually involves no force and often no 
technical intrusion; it relies on persuading the 
victim to act against his or her own interest.27 
Unsolicited Messaging 
An unsolicited message is an electronic 
communication sent without the recipient’s prior 
request or consent, and the Act itself defines 
unsolicited messages in exactly these terms.28 
Such messages reach users through SMS, 
WhatsApp, social media and fraudulent calls. Not 
every unsolicited message is unlawful; the 
concern here is with those used to open a 
fraudulent exchange. In Tanzania, the typical 
message announces a prize, a mistaken transfer, 
an approved loan or an urgent need to ‘verify’ the 
account.29 Unsolicited messaging is the principal

Effectiveness of the Cybercrimes Act 
Effectiveness refers to the extent to which the Act 
achieves its objectives of preventing, detecting, 
investigating, prosecuting and deterring 
cybercrime. Following Goldbarsht and de Koker, 
it depends on five interrelated factors: legislative 
adequacy, institutional capacity, technological 
capability, cooperation among stakeholders and 
public awareness.30 Fuller’s account of the 
morality of law explains why the first factor 
cannot be traded off against the others: a statute 
may be clearly drafted yet ineffective if the 
institutions cannot apply it, and strong institutions 
cannot compensate for a rule that fails to describe 
the conduct it is meant to punish. Hart adds that a 
rule of primary obligation also needs secondary

change it.31 Effectiveness is therefore the central 
evaluative concept of the study, and it links the 
other four: mobile money is the platform, the 
unsolicited message is the mechanism, fraud is the

METHODOLOGY 
Research Design 
The study adopted a mixed-methods design that 
combined doctrinal legal analysis with empirical 
data collection. Doctrinal research identifies, 
analyses, and synthesises the content of the law,32 
and it can show what the Act says and where its 
text is ambiguous or silent. It cannot, however,

actually able to use the Act. The empirical 
component was included to capture those

Study Area 
Fieldwork took place in Dodoma City. Dodoma

combination allowed the study to obtain informed 
institutional views while also hearing from 
ordinary users who had experienced fraud.

Abstract
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) are the biggest paradigm shift in the Indian approach towards crime, procedure and evidence. This research paper brings a detailed doctrinal and analytical analysis of the legal regime for cyber crimes and digital evidence under these three changing legislations in place of Indian Evidence Act, Indian Penal Code and Code of Criminal Procedure that has remained unchanged for more than one hundred and fifty years. The study traces the evolution of norms from IPC/IT Act to BNS, and breaks down the legislation related to online fraud, identity theft, phishing, cyberstalking, digital impersonation, ransomware, deepfake misuse and social media offences. Critically reviews the requirements for admissibility of electronic records in the BSA, 2023, including Sections 61–63, which cover certification, expert testimony rules, and metadata, cloud data and forensic outputs. The paper also discusses procedural safeguards to ensure integrity of the digital evidence collection procedures, the chain of custody and the role of cyber forensic laboratories in the BNSS. The study highlights the ongoing anxieties of courts regarding the reliability of electronic evidence as identified through an analysis of landmark cases, namely, Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014), Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020), and further cases. It then addresses border issues, such as cross-border jurisdiction, encryption, AI-generated content authentication, preservation of evidence using blockchain, and data privacy issues stemming from the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The paper ends with a multi-dimensional framework of reform which brings together technological, legislative and institutional suggestions for India to build a strong digital justice framework.

Keywords: Cyber Crime, Digital Evidence, BNS 2023, 
BSA 2023, BNSS 2023, Electronic Records, Cyber 
Forensics, Digital Justice, Artificial Intelligence, 
Blockchain, and Cyber Security. 
 
 
 
 
I. INTRODUCTION 
 
The digitalization of society has led to a rapid 
increase in cybercrime over the last decades, putting 
current laws unable to meet the challenges of the 21st 
century criminal threat. India as one of the fastest-
growing digital economies in the world with more 
than 900 million internet users and a Unified 
Payments interface (UPI) system that handled 
billions of transactions last year makes it 
exceptionally vulnerable to cyber criminality. As 
indicated in the latest report of the National Crime 
Records Bureau (NCRB) on Cyber Crime Report 
2023, the number of cybercrime complaints has 
increased by 113.7% compared to 2021, with 15.92 
lakh complaints made.  
 
In this background, Parliament passed three ground-
breaking legislations in 2023 – Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), Bharatiya Nagrik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), effective from 1 July 2024. 
These laws superseded the Indian Penal Code, 1860 
(IPC), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC), 
and Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (IEA) respectively. 
The BNS trilogy complements and significantly 
restructures the substantive and procedural 
framework for the investigation of digital offences, in 
addition to the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT 
Act) and its Amendment in 2008.   
      
This research paper consists of nine parts. This 
Introduction is followed by Section 2 which traces 
the history of cybercrime law in India. Section 3 
deals with the mapping of cyber offences as provided 
in the BNS with cross reference analysis to IT Act. 
Section 4 dissects the admissibility of digital 
evidence under the BSA. The BNSS procedural 
safeguards are explored in Section 5. Section 6 
examines key case law. Explores frontier

technological challenges for Section 7. Section 8 
outlines comparative frameworks internationally. A

II. EVOLUTION OF CYBERCRIME 
REGULATION: FROM IPC TO BNS 
 
2.1 The IPC Era: Analogical Application and Its 
Limits 
Before the Information Technology Act, 2000, the 
law enforcement authorities and courts in India had 
been making use of IPC, 1860 in an analogical 
manner to deal with cyber-enabled offences. The 
Victorian-era IPC sections of 420 (cheating), 463 
(forgery), 499 (defamation) and 354A (sexual 
harassment) were all put to the test for crimes they 
could not have foreseen. This resulted in doctrinal 
incoherence – in State of Tamil Nadu v. Suhas Katti 
(2004), the Supreme Court found IPC's provisions for 
cyberspace offences as inadequate and called for 
specialised legislation.  
 
There were three basic constraints with this time. The 
first being territorial jurisdiction principles under 
section 2 of IPC were unable to cope with the 
'borderless' aspect of cyberspace. Second, the term 
‘document’ in Section 29 IPC was expanded by the 
courts, but still not clear with regard to electronic 
documents. Third, the lack of computer-specific 
mens rea – such as knowledge of vulnerability to a 
system, for example – imposed new challenges for 
prosecutors which defence counsel exploited 
systematically.  
 
2.2 The IT Act Framework: Partial Codification 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended 
in 2008) enacted specific offences for hacking 
(Section 66), identity theft (Section 66C), phishing 
(Section 66D), cyber stalking (Section 66A – 
subsequently struck down in Shreya Singhal v. Union 
of India, 2015), voyeurism (Section 66E) and 
publication of obscene material in electronic form 
(Section 67). Section 65 was dedicated to tampering 
with computer source documents. But the scope of 
the IT Act was not full as it could not cover 
ransomware, deepfakes, cryptocurrency fraud, social 
engineering or the whole category of offences 
through the social media platforms.  
 
The Supreme Court held that the definition of 
‘grossly offensive' in Section 66A of IT Act was 
vague and that it denied freedom of expression as 
guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution 
of India in Shreya Singhal case.In the Shreya Singhal 
case [(2015) 5 SCC 1] the Supreme Court struck 
down the critical provision of Section 66A of the IT 
Act, which made communication of a “grossly 
offensive” message a criminal offense, for 
unconstitutional vagueness and disproportionate 
interference with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. 
This judgment highlighted a huge lacuna in the 
Indian cyber law ecosystem, as there wasn't anything 
for the enforcement agencies to take action against 
incitement to violence, hate speech and harassment in 
the digital world.  
 
2.3 The BNS, 2023: A New Architecture 
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does not 
specifically address the issue of cyber crimes and 
rather also adds to the existing definitions of offence 
categories with cyber elements and also includes a 
few new clauses with cyber dimensions. The key 
changes from the IPC are: (i) explicit reference to 
electronic and digital as means of commission for a 
number of offences; (ii) increased penalties for 
offences involving digital platforms; (iii) inclusion of 
deepfake and AI generated content in the fraud and 
defamation offences; and (iv) a new alternative 
sentence of community service — a provision with 
indirect ramifications for minor cyber offences.

III. CYBER OFFENCES UNDER THE 
BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA, 2023 
 
3.1 Online Fraud and Financial Cybercrime 
Section 318 BNS brings together the definitions of 
cheating, and explicitly expands them to digital 
transactions. The section makes it criminal to induce 
a person to deliver or to change or destroy a valuable 
security by any deceitful act, such as electronic 
communication. Financial cybercrime — which 
includes UPI fraud, OTP theft, phishing, vishing and 
card-not-present fraud — is clearly covered by 
Section 318 under Section 66D of IT Act 
(punishment for cheating by personation using 
computer resources). The BNS codifies the Supreme 
Court's rulings in Tukaram S. Dighole v. Manikrao 
Shivaji Kokate [(2010) 4 SCC 329] in affirming that 
electronic communication can be the "deceptive 
inducement" necessary for cheatings.  
 
Ransomware attacks involve more than one 
provision: BNS Section 308 BNS (extortion), BNS 
Section 66 IT Act (hacking), and possibly BNS 
Section 385 BNS (putting persons in fear of injury). 
However, a lack of a specific ransomware offence 
does make prosecuting the composite mens rea of 
these provisions challenging.   
 
3.2 Identity Theft and Digital Impersonation 
Section 319 BNS Cheating by personation is covered 
in Section 319 BNS, which has been updated from 
Section 416 IPC to include digital identity fraud. This 
is in addition to Section 66C of the IT Act (identity 
theft using electronic signature, password or other 
unique identification feature). The Delhi High Court 
in Avnish Bajaj v. State (NCT of Delhi) [(2008) 150 
DLT 769] had grappled with the intermediary 
liability issue for hosted identity-fraudulent content, 
which section 79 of the IT Act and the 2023 
Intermediary Guidelines partially address.  
 
The biggest threat that is currently facing us is deep 
fake fraud. Unlike the BNS or the IT Act, there is no 
specific provision that addresses the use of AI-
generated synthetic media – photorealistic video 
fabrication of real people. The current legal response 
consists of Section 319 BNS (personation) 
incorporated with Section 356 BNS (defamation) 
with Section 67A IT Act (obscene electronic content 
of a sexual nature) and civil remedies under the new 
right to one's likeness. The problem is severe: 
Globally, deepfake pornography of women has more 
than tripled in the last 5 years alone, from 2019 to 
2024, and warrants immediate legislative measures.   
 
3.3 Cyberstalking and Online Harassment 
Section 78 BNS clearly draws in online 
communication and digital surveillance under its 
definition, which is a major improvement over 
Section 354D IPC, which was progressive but lacked 
specificity of digital modes. Section 75 BNS deals 
specifically with sexual harassment, where digital 
platforms are used, with more severe penalties. In the 
case of Shilpa Mittal v State of Maharashtra, the 
Bombay High Court highlighted the mental trauma 
that can be caused by the continuous harassment on 
the internet and the importance of the BNS's wider 
interpretation of the term.  
 
The provisions of the BNS does not completely fill 
the existing lacuna in the provisions of the IT Act due 
to the invalidation of Section 66A of the IT Act. In 
the absence of these some portions are replaced by 
the provisions of Section 353(2) BNS (statements 
conducing to public mischief) and Section 197 BNS 
(imputations prejudicial to national integration), but 
their constitutional validity and scope is debatable in 
light of the Shreya Singhal framework. The BNS 
drafters have not reached a clear conclusion as to the

and Article 19(1)(a) protections for free expression.  
 
3.4 Social Media Offences and Platform 
Accountability 
The BNS defines social media offences as 
defamation by electronic communication (Section 
356), criminal intimidation by electronic 
communication (Section 351), incitement through 
electronic communication (Section 353) and 
obscenity (Section 294 BNS read with Section 67 IT 
Act). One of the most important is Section 336 BNS 
which makes any act that poses a risk to personal 
safety, life and health illegal, such as coordinated 
online harassment campaigns, doxxing (public 
disclosure of private information) and swatting. 
 
Accountability of the platform for user-generated 
content remains largely under the Regulation of 
sections 79 of the IT Act and Information 
Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital 
Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021. The BNS does not 
change this and establishes an additional liability risk 
to the downstream parties where platforms can 
demonstrably not perform their duty of care and 
offences leading to a death or grievous hurt are 
directly caused by the content they host.   
 
IV. DIGITAL EVIDENCE UNDER THE 
BHARATIYA SAKSHYA ADHINIYAM, 
2023 
 
4.1 Framework and Definitional Architecture 
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 is the most 
profound overhaul of the evidence law in India since 
the Indian Evidence Act of 1872. Digital justice, as a 
key element of the BSA, is a comprehensive 
definitional and admissibility regime for electronic 
records, which overcomes some doctrinal ambiguities 
that had arisen with the amended Evidence Act 
provisions (Sections 65A and 65B IEA) inserted in 
2000.   
 
Section 2(1)(d) BSA expressly defines ‘document' as 
including electronic and digital records, emails, log 
data from servers, locational data, SMS/messaging 
application data, voice messages, video messages, 
electronic contracts, website content and anything 
stored or processed in a digital format. The broad 
definition addresses the previous judicial confusion 
over the definition of ‘documents' for evidentiary 
purposes regarding certain types of digital data, such 
as metadata, cache files, and ephemeral 
communications.  
 
4.2 Admissibility of Electronic Records: Sections 61–
63 BSA 
These provisions are the BSA's central provisions on 
admissibility of electronic records, which 
considerably restructure the provisions of Sections 
65A and 65B of the IEA. The new framework makes 
the following key modifications:   
 
• The admissibility of documents was previously 
split between ‘primary’ evidence and ‘secondary’ 
evidence which gave rise to complicated 
admissibility hierarchies, but section 61 BSA now 
unites them under a single umbrella, provided 
they meet the conditions set out in that section.  
• Section 62 BSA states the requirements for 
admissibility of electronic records: (a) the 
computer/device output is generated by a person 
with lawful control over the computer in the 
normal course of that person's activities; (b) the 
computer or device is operating properly, or if 
not, that the operating error does not affect the 
output; (c) the information contained in the record 
is regularly entered in the computer in the normal 
course of the activities of the person; and (d) a 
certificate of compliance signed by a responsible 
official is obtained.  
• Section 63 BSA covers how to ensure the 
authenticity of electronic records and provides 
standards for multi-factor authentication, which 
include digital signatures, hash values and 
metadata verification.  
 
An innovation feature of Section 62 BSA is that it 
explicitly recognises cloud computing environments, 
in contrast to the previous Section 65B IEA. The 
former provision had caused some interpretative 
difficulty in instances where evidence may be stored 
on distributed cloud servers, where the BSA's more 
general language referring to 'computer resource' as 
defined by the IT Act covers the situation.

4.3 Certificate Requirement: Continuing and New 
Challenges 
The certificate requirement, which is perhaps the 
most litigated element of the admissibility of 
electronic evidence in India, has been considerably 
clarified by the BSA and remains a jurisprudential 
contentious element. The certificate required by 
Section 62(2) BSA shall be signed by a person in a 
responsible official position in connection with the 
operation of the relevant device and shall contain: (i) 
a description of the manner of production of the 
electronic record; (ii) particulars of the device in 
question; and (iii) a statement that to the best of the 
signatory's knowledge and belief, the conditions of 
Section 62(1) are met.  
 
The Supreme Court in the Arjun Panditrao Khotkar 
vs. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal supreme court case 
(2020) 7 SCC 1, has held that the certificate under 
Section 65B(4) IEA (now Section 62 BSA) is a sine 
qua non and cannot be waived even by the courts for 
the admissibility of electronic records. The Court also 
explained that the certificate must be tendered at the 
time of electronic record's deposition and cannot be 
tendered later. The BSA formalizes this holding and 
adds the beneficial rule that, when it is impossible to 
obtain a certificate from the certificate-maker (e.g., in 
the case of a foreign server), the court may be 
satisfied with secondary evidence or draw 
appropriate inferences.  
 
4.4 Types of Digital Evidence: Specific Evidentiary 
Standards 
4.4.1 Metadata and Log Files 
Mtadata — includes file creation dates, modification 
logs, author information, EXIF data in photographs, 
routing information in email messages, system log 
files and more. The BSA does not mention the term 
‘metadata’ directly, but it does discuss this concept 
by the general term ‘electronic record’ and the 
authentication requirements in Section 63. In view of 
the evidentiary value of metadata, courts have 
increasingly accepted it as evidence with proper 
certification: In Dharambir v. CBI [(2008) 150 DLT 
393], the Delhi High Court allowed computer-
generated logs as evidence with appropriate 
certification. 
 
4.4.2 CCTV Footage and Video Evidence 
CCTV footage has specific challenges with 
authenticity: it can be compromised by compression, 
low resolution, editing of the time stamp, and 
conversion of the format of the footage. Where a 
BSA Section 79 (presumption as to electronic 
agreements and records) or a BSA Section 81 
(presumption as to electronic messages) is in effect, 
the system is subject to these presumptions. In 
Tomaso Bruno v. State of U.P. [(2015) 7 SCC 178], 
the Supreme Court accepted CCTV footage as 
evidence of corroboration and stressed the need for a 
chain of custody and expert analysis of the footage.  
 
4.4.3 Mobile Device Data and Social Media 
Communications 
One of the most vibrant fields of digital evidence law 
is the preservation and admission of mobile device 
information: call history, WhatsApp conversations, 
deleted text messages retrieved via mobile device 
forensics, geospatial data, and so on. The Madras 
High Court in the case of Dharani Sugars and 
Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India noted that 
WhatsApp messages can be admissible with the 
proper certification but it has to be established that 
the extraction of such messages is done in a manner 
that is proper and proper linkage with the accused has 
been done. While the BSA's Section 62 framework is 
uniform across mobile-extracted data, practical issues 
of end-to-end encryption can lead to being able to 
extract metadata but not necessarily the content of a 
message.  
 
4.4.4 Cloud-Stored Evidence 
Cloud computing's distributed and multi-
jurisdictional design presents significant issues for 
digital evidence law. Amazon Web Services, Google 
Cloud, Microsoft Azure and other providers may 
store data on servers in different countries, which 
could raise issues around territorial jurisdiction in 
gathering evidence, potential issues with foreign data 
protection laws (such as the GDPR) and whether the 
Indian procedural rules would apply to foreign 
service providers. The BSA's Section 62 takes a 
pragmatic approach and allows the 'person in control' 
of the computer resource to certify it without having 
to specify any particular physical location of a server, 
thereby addressing the jurisdiction issue somewhat.

V. PROCEDURAL SAFEGUARDS UNDER 
THE BHARATIYA NAGARIK SURAKSHA 
SANHITA, 2023 
5.1 Search, Seizure, and Preservation of Digital 
Evidence 
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 brings 
in significantly updated provisions regarding the 
search and seizure of electronic evidence to fill in 
some major gaps in the previous CrPC provisions, 
which were drafted before the extensive use of 
computers in criminal activity. Section 94 BNSS 
provides for the compelling production of documents 
and digital records, and there are new sub-provisions 
that specifically cover electronic devices, cloud 
accounts and remote servers.    
 
The current section 185 BNSS is complemented by 
section 186, which introduces for the first time the 
notion of digital search warrants, that is court orders 
that permit access to electronic devices, email 
accounts, cloud storage and encrypted data. The 
procedural requirements are: particular identification 
of the target device, specification of the categories of 
data sought, the limitation of the scope of the search 
over the course of time and required videography of 
the search process. Section 105 BNSS's videography 
requirement also has an impact on digital evidence 
because it will result in a contemporaneous record of 
the forensic acquisition process, which will enhance 
chain-of-custody integrity.   
 
5.2 Chain of Custody and Digital Forensic Standards 
The chain of custody, a documented continuous chain 
of possession, condition and location from the time of 
seizure to court presentation, is critical to the 
integrity of digital evidence. The BNSS introduces 
Section 530 which requires the preparation of a 
'Digital Evidence Recovery Sheet' (DERS) at the 
time of electronic device seizure, including 
identification of device (IMEI, serial number, MAC 
address), condition of device, storage capacity and 
contents, device encryption, and forensic acquisition 
technique used.  
 
In addition, the BNSS requires, in Section 531, that 
all digital evidence handling be done with write-
blocking equipment to ensure that any original data is 
not accidentally altered, and that a forensic image 
(bit-for-bit copy) be created prior to any analysis with 
hash values (MD5 or SHA-256) also calculated for 
both the original image and the forensic image to 
ensure that they are identical. Such a codification of 
good practice forensics is welcome progress, but the 
success or otherwise of the law will rely heavily on 
the equipment available and the training of country-
wide police forensic units, which is a shortage in 
smaller states and union territories.    
 
5.3 Trial Procedure and Electronic Evidence 
Presentation 
Section 353(3) of the BNSS allows for electronic 
evidence to be presented at trial, allowing witnesses 
to testify via video link and documents to be 
displayed electronically, with proper authentication. 
With electronic filing of case documents and 
chargesheets under Section 530 BNSS, an all 
electronic evidentiary system in principle has been 
made possible by the BSA's electronic record 
provisions.    
 
Perhaps most importantly, the BNSS has introduced a 
requirement for the mandatory forensic investigation 
of offences, where seven or more years imprisonment 
will be imposed, in Section 176(3): this includes the 
filming of the investigation of any crime scene by a 
forensic team. This is a measure which is in its main 
form directed at physical crime scenes, but which 
practitioners interpret as covering digital crime 
scenes (servers, devices, networks) in light of the 
definition of 'crime scene' as being integrated in the 
BNSS's Explanation to Section 176.  
 
VI. LANDMARK JUDICIAL PRECEDENTS 
ON DIGITAL EVIDENCE 
 
6.1 Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer: The Foundational 
Ruling 
The three-judge bench interpretation by the Supreme 
Court in Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer [(2014) 10 SCC 
473] has basically changed the rules of admissibility 
of electronic evidence in India. In State (NCT of 
Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu (2005), the earlier division 
bench had clarified that secondary evidence 
provisions will be applicable in the admission of

Financial institutions now face attacks directed not only at technical authentication, but also at the social cues through which customers and employees decide whom to trust. This study combines descriptive analysis of public United States fraud statistics with directed qualitative content analysis of 18 (eighteen) authoritative regulatory, law-enforcement, standards, and policy documents published between 2019 and 2025. Incident response appeared in about 94% of the corpus while identity verification stood at 89%. Human authentication and transaction monitoring were present in 83% and 72%, respectively. Deepfake Enabled Financial Fraud and Consumer Trust in Digital Finance: Can 
Vulnerability–Trust–Resilience Framework Be Applied in the United States of 
America? 
 
Nenbee, Simeon Gbimoiye (PhD)1, Golley, Israel Tega2, Mgbataogu, Ifeanyi Sunday (PhD)3 
1Department of Economics, University of Port Harcourt 
2Graduate School of Economics and Management University of Port Harcourt, https://orcid.org/0009-0008-2609-8612 
3Department of Finance and Banking, University of Port Harcourt 
    
ABSTRACT: Generative artificial intelligence has made convincing synthetic identities, voices, images, and video cheaper and easier to 
produce. Financial institutions now face attacks directed not only at technical authentication, but also at the social cues through which 
customers and employees decide whom to trust. This study combines descriptive analysis of public United States fraud statistics with 
directed qualitative content analysis of 18 (eighteen) authoritative regulatory, law-enforcement, standards, and policy documents 
published between 2019 and 2025. Eight response mechanisms were coded: accountable ownership, identity verification, deepfake 
detection and provenance, transaction monitoring, human authentication and escalation, customer information, incident response 
and information sharing, and third-party governance. Incident response appeared in about 94% of the corpus while identity 
verification stood at 89%. Human authentication and transaction monitoring were present in 83% and 72%, respectively. Half of the 
documents addressed provenance or deepfake detection, whereas only 39% connected counter-fraud controls with customer 
communication. Public loss data confirm a rapidly worsening fraud environment but do not identify losses caused specifically by 
deepfakes, producing an attribution-denominator problem. The proposed Vulnerability–Trust–Resilience (VTR) framework shows how 
synthetic media can turn weaknesses in authentication and judgment into financial loss and wider distrust. Resilience therefore 
depends on layered verification, transaction-context controls, empowered human escalation, rapid recovery, and carefully calibrated 
communication—not on a single detector. It is therefore recommend that there is need to urgently develop testable propositions, a 
managerial scorecard, and a reproducible engagement agenda by the government to forestall the growing incidence of deekfake 
enabled financial fraud in the financial sector of the economy. 
KEYWORDS: Deepfake fraud; consumer trust; digital finance; identity verification and generative artificial intelligence 
 
1. INTRODUCTION 
Digital finance rests on trust that must function at scale to various categories of customers. Customers often times open accounts 
remotely, authorize payments on mobile devices, obtain advice through electronic channels, and increasingly communicate with 
automated agents. Most customers are employees in the digital finance space and make consequential decisions using video meetings, 
telephone calls, emailed instructions, identity documents, and digital signatures. In each instance, the institution converts incomplete 
identity and behavioral signals into judgments about access, credit, payment, and responsibility. In recent years, generative Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) alters the economics of attacking those judgments. Faces, voices, documents, and persuasive dialogue can now be 
synthesized or manipulated cheaply, across languages, and at operational scale thereby posing threat to consumption patterns and 
habits. 
The threat extends well beyond conspicuous fabricated video. FinCEN (2024a) reported increasing suspicious activity involving 
suspected deepfake media in schemes directed at institutions and their customers, including altered or fabricated identity documents 
intended to defeat verification and authentication. Synthetic voices can even make impersonation more credible in such senerios. 
Deepfake Enabled Financial Fraud and Consumer Trust in Digital Finance: Can Vulnerability–Trust–Resilience 
Framework Be Applied in the United States of America? 
JEFMS, Volume 09 Issue 09 September 2026                                       www.ijefm.co.in                                                Page 4999 
Manipulated faces may target onboarding or liveness controls. Generated documents can facilitate account takeover, mule-account 
creation, and payment fraud, while personalized messages make social engineering harder to recognize. The appropriate unit of 
analysis is therefore the fraud process—not the media artifact in isolation—from reconnaissance and persuasion through identity 
compromise, transaction execution, and concealment. 
The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3, 2025) did received 859,532 complaints for the year 2024 
and $16.6 billion in losses—33% above the 2023 total. Those figures are not a measure of deepfake losses; incident reports do not 
consistently record whether synthetic media played a role. They do, however, describe the environment into which scalable 
impersonation technology has entered.  
One sense about the IC3( 2025) report is that the aggregate fraud statistics establish urgency and exposure, but they cannot estimate 
the marginal causal contribution of deepfakes. The damage can extend beyond direct victimization. Once customers believe that 
voices, faces, documents, or institutional messages can be fabricated at will, legitimate interactions become harder and more 
expensive to verify. Some may delay valid transfers or retreat from remote channels; others may encounter a “liar’s dividend”, the 
term Chesney & Citron (2019) use for the way public awareness of synthetic media lets wrongdoers dismiss genuine, incriminating 
evidence as fake. More specifically, institutional responses can create their own harms if added friction excludes customers without 
advanced devices, stable connectivity, conventional identity records, or accessible biometric options. Governance must therefore 
pursue two objectives at once: prevent successful fraud and preserve justified confidence and equitable access. 
Arising from the above, latitudes of research on deepfakes are dispersed across various disciplines like computer science, 
cybersecurity, criminology, psychology, information systems, and sorts. These fields frequently examine different parts of the same 
problem. Detection studies tend to report benchmark accuracy under controlled conditions, whereas fraud advisories concentrate on 
operational red flags. Trust research on the hand explores reliance on technology but seldom follows the consumer through post-
incident recovery while financial-risk documents acknowledge cyber and model risk without always separating synthetic-media 
controls from conventional anti-fraud practice. This fragmentation leaves three gaps: First, detection alone cannot carry the control 
burden. A classifier may perform strongly on familiar generation methods and then deteriorate after compression, adversarial 
alteration, model change, or deployment in a different population. Losses also arise when a customer or employee follows a persuasive 
instruction that no detector ever evaluates. Effective defense must span identity, device, behavior, transaction context, human 
challenge, and recovery. Second, consumer trust is often treated as an attitude rather than an outcome shaped by governance. 
Confidence may be damaged by the original fraud, but also by the institution’s response, unclear warnings, mistaken account 
restrictions, or a burdensome reimbursement process. Proportionate and understandable controls can reinforce trust. Repeated false 
positives and unequal exclusion can erode it. Third, the empirical denominator is missing. Public systems record complaint categories 
and losses, while institutions apply heterogeneous internal labels. “Deepfake-enabled” may mean that synthetic media was essential 
to the scheme, that it merely strengthened persuasion, or that its use was suspected but unconfirmed. Without a stable taxonomy, 
prevalence, institutional comparison, and control effectiveness remain difficult to estimate.  
Accordingly, this paper sets to provide answers to the following questions and more: (a) Which organizational and technical response 
mechanisms recur in authoritative guidance on synthetic-media and digitally enabled financial fraud? (b)  Where should the current 
frameworks under-specify consumer trust, content provenance, and outcome be measured?  and (c)Through what pathways do 
deepfake-enabled attacks and institutional responses affect adoption, confidence, inclusion, and resilience in digital finance? These 
questions and more are interrogated in this study. The rest of the paper addresses literature review, methodology, results and 
discussion and concluding remarks. 
 
2. LITERATURE REVIEW 
2.1 Survey of Theoretical Literature 
Routine activity theory explains predatory events as a convergence of motivated offenders, suitable targets, and insufficient 
guardianship (Cohen & Felson, 1979). Digital finance broadens the reach of potential targets and permits remote contact; generative 
AI adds credibility and scale. Guardianship, however, is distributed across the system. A customer may question an unusual request, a 
bank may detect anomalous device behavior, a telecommunications provider may restrict spoofing, and law enforcement may 
combine reports across victims. This perspective directs analysis away from the artifact alone and toward the opportunity structure 
surrounding it. 
Deepfake Enabled Financial Fraud and Consumer Trust in Digital Finance: Can Vulnerability–Trust–Resilience 
Framework Be Applied in the United States of America? 
JEFMS, Volume 09 Issue 09 September 2026                                       www.ijefm.co.in                                                Page 5000 
Protection motivation theory helps explain why some warnings prompt useful action and others do not. People assess both the 
seriousness of a threat and whether an effective, manageable response is available (Rogers, 1975). Deepfake warnings may improve 
behavior when customers recognize a credible risk and know how to respond. Alarm without a practical verification step may instead 
create helplessness or generalized distrust. Customer education should therefore strengthen response efficacy and self-efficacy. 
Telling people to distrust everything is unworkable; instructing them to verify unusual payment requests through a known, 
independent channel is actionable. 
Trust in automation research distinguishes appropriate reliance from maximal reliance. Lee and See (2004) define trust as an attitude 
that an agent will help achieve goals under uncertainty and show that calibration matters. Under-trust wastes useful automation; 
over-trust creates misuse. Deepfake fraud produces a related calibration problem across channels: consumers and employees must 
neither accept every audiovisual cue nor reject all legitimate remote interaction. Institutions support calibration by displaying 
meaningful signals, explaining protective processes, and providing recovery when signals fail. 
Organizational resilience concerns the capacity to anticipate, absorb, recover from, and adapt after disruption. Synthetic-media fraud 
is adaptive: controls alter offender behavior, new generation tools appear, and attacks migrate between channels. Resilience therefore 
requires feedback from complaints, confirmed cases, false positives, customer outcomes, and external intelligence. A static annual 
policy is insufficient when attack signatures change weekly. 
Institution-based trust adds the rules, safeguards, and structural assurances surrounding a transaction (McKnight et al., 2002). 
Customers need not understand a detection model to judge whether a bank provides credible safeguards, understandable notices, 
accessible escalation, and fair remediation. This perspective makes trust an outcome of governance design rather than merely 
communication or brand reputation. 
The Vulnerability–Trust–Resilience (VTR) framework developed in this article joins these perspectives. Vulnerability occurs when 
synthetic content exploits dependence on familiar signals, procedural gaps, urgency, or authority. Trust is shaped by the attack and 
by what the institution visibly does afterward. Resilience appears when controls break the fraud chain, contain loss, restore legitimate 
access, and turn incidents into learning. The proposed routes to value are therefore interruption, calibration, recovery, and adaptation. 
Inferencing the expressed views in literature, a joint advisory from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the Federal 
Bureau of Investigation, and the National Security Agency (2023) framed deepfakes as a cross-sector organizational risk rather than a 
purely technical curiosity, recommending governance, detection, and incident-response measures in combination. It is pertinent to 
ascertain the Case-based scholarship which reinforces this organizational framing. In de Rancourt-Raymond & Smaili’s (2023) work 
that examined publicly reported corporate deepfake-fraud incidents, it argued that the ethical and governance failures exposed by 
these cases extend well beyond any single technical detection gap. Early deepfake research concentrated on generation and detection. 
The technical literature describes an arms race: artifacts that reveal one generation method can disappear in later models, while 
distribution through platforms alters resolution and strips metadata. NIST (2024b) accordingly treats provenance, watermarking, 
detection, testing, and incident disclosure as complementary controls rather than promising a definitive classifier. Accuracy measured 
on a balanced laboratory dataset also does not translate directly into positive predictive value when attacks are rare. Even a strong 
detector may overwhelm reviewers when genuine interactions vastly outnumber fraudulent ones. 
Identity research emphasizes document authenticity, biometrics, presentation-attack detection, and liveness. These controls address 
remote onboarding and account access, but each has boundary conditions. Biometric systems may perform differently across 
demographic groups, accessibility conditions, devices, and environments. Active liveness challenges add friction and may be imitated 
or socially engineered. Document checks can fail when synthetic identities combine real and fabricated elements. Layering is therefore 
essential: identity evidence should be connected to device reputation, behavioral patterns, account history, and transaction purpose. 
The scale of the underlying problem is already substantial: FinCEN's (2024b) analysis of Bank Secrecy Act filings found that identity-
related concerns accounted for 42% of suspicious activity reports in 2021, representing $212 billion in suspicious activity, most 
commonly involving impersonation intended to defeat verification. 
Fraud management adds transaction monitoring and case investigation. An authenticated person can still be manipulated into 
authorizing a payment, and a deepfake can target an employee outside customer-login controls. Contextual signals—new beneficiary, 
unusual amount, time pressure, channel switching, device change, atypical location, or inconsistent narrative—may remain 
informative even when audiovisual content looks authentic. FinCEN’s (2024a) red flags reflect this system view by combining media 
anomalies, identity inconsistencies, device indicators, and transaction behavior.

Framework Be Applied in the United States of America? 
JEFMS, Volume 09 Issue 09 September 2026                                       www.ijefm.co.in                                                Page 5001 
Cybersecurity guidance emphasizes preparation and information sharing. The U.S. Department of the Treasury (2024a) identified data 
supply-chain, third-party, and capability gaps affecting financial-sector management of AI-specific cyber risks, while a companion 
report on broader AI adoption in financial services documented similar concerns around data quality, third-party dependence, and 
workforce capability (U.S. Department of the Treasury, 2024b). NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework organizes activity around 
govern, map, measure, and manage (NIST, 2023), while the generative-AI profile applies those functions to risks including 
confabulation, information integrity, privacy, and security (NIST, 2024a). These frameworks support lifecycle governance but are not 
specialized fraud-loss measurement standards. The International Organization for Standardization's (2023) AI management-system 
standard complements this lifecycle view by specifying organizational processes for risk assessment and continual improvement, while 
the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity's (2022) threat-landscape analysis situates deepfake-enabled fraud within a broader 
pattern of AI-enabled cybercrime observed across European institutions. Reflecting similar concerns domestically, the Federal Reserve 
Board (2025) has highlighted deepfakes as an emerging element of the bank cybersecurity arms race, requiring institutions to treat 
synthetic-media risk as a standing agenda item rather than a periodic review topic. 
Financial-stability analysis broadens the scope. The FSB (2024) identifies AI-related vulnerabilities involving third-party dependencies, 
cyber risks, market correlations, and model risk, data quality, and governance. It also recognizes that generative AI can increase fraud 
and disinformation. The systemic concern is not simply that one customer is deceived, but that common providers, shared 
authentication assumptions, or synchronized misinformation could produce correlated losses and runs on confidence. The Financial 
Action Task Force (2023) situates this concern within the broader landscape of cyber-enabled fraud, noting that illicit proceeds 
increasingly move through layered digital channels that blend social engineering, compromised credentials, and rapid fund transfers, 
complicating both detection and recovery. 
Consumer trust scholarship suggests that competence, benevolence, integrity, predictability, and structural assurance matter. After 
fraud, customers observe whether an institution responds promptly, communicates respectfully, explains decisions, restores access, 
and allocates loss fairly. A technically successful control that repeatedly locks out legitimate customers can lower trust, especially 
among vulnerable groups. Conversely, transparent verification can signal competence. Security and customer experience are not 
separate workstreams; they jointly determine perceived reliability. Experimental evidence from adjacent digital-trust research 
supports this pattern: Muzatko & Bansal (2024) find that prompt, transparent breach disclosure combined with concrete protective 
measures restores consumer trust more effectively than delayed or vague communication, reinforcing that the manner and speed of 
institutional response, not only the incident itself, shapes post-incident trust. 
Public fraud statistics establish scale but offer weak attribution to a specific mechanism. IC3 reports losses across cyber-enabled crime, 
and the Federal Trade Commission (2025) aggregates consumer reports across fraud categories. Underreporting, awareness, duplicate 
or incomplete records, and classification decisions all affect these systems. Their proper interpretation is as indicators of reported loss, 
not estimates of population prevalence. Most importantly, historical records do not contain a consistent deepfake field. A precise 
national estimate of deepfake-caused losses is therefore not credible without case-level classification. 
The literature seemingly reveals five gaps. They are: (i) technical detection is weakly integrated with transaction and organizational 
controls. (ii), trust is rarely measured before and after an incident using comparable instruments. (iii), deepfake involvement lacks 
standardized reporting levels. (iv), false-positive, accessibility, and inclusion costs are underdeveloped. (v), few studies connect control 
maturity to verified loss reduction using longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs. The present review organizes convergent 
mechanisms and makes these missing quantities explicit. 
 
3. METHODOLOGY 
This paper uses a structured integrative review with directed qualitative content analysis and descriptive statistics secondary-data 
analysis. This approach is appropriate because the research question concerns institutional convergence and conceptual integration 
across heterogeneous authoritative sources. It does not estimate causal effects or population prevalence. The unit of analysis for 
qualitative coding is one public document. The quantitative component consists of code frequencies and reported-loss trends 
reproduced from official sources. 
The analysis followed five stages: problem formulation; transparent source identification; eligibility screening; deductive coding with 
documented decision rules; and synthesis through frequencies, co-occurrence, negative cases, and theory building. The review is

Framework Be Applied in the United States of America?

structured rather than claimed as a systematic review of all academic literature. Its corpus intentionally prioritizes documents with 
direct authority over financial, cybersecurity, identity, fraud, or consumer-protection practice. 
3.2 Population and Sampling 
The conceptual population comprises English-language public guidance, standards, reports, alerts, and strategy documents addressing 
synthetic media, generative-AI security, digital identity, cyber-enabled fraud, or financial-sector AI risk. Purposive maximum-variation 
sampling was used across issuer type and jurisdiction. Sources were eligible if they (a) were issued by a regulator, law-enforcement 
body, standards institution, intergovernmental body, or financial authority; (b) contained operational recommendations or 
documented threat evidence; (c) were available in full; and (d) were published from 2019 through 2025, with foundational identity or 
cybersecurity guidance retained when necessary. 
Documents were excluded when they were promotional vendor material, duplicated another source, offered commentary without 
traceable evidence, or mentioned AI without a relevant fraud, identity, cyber, or trust mechanism. Eighteen documents were retained. 
U.S. sources were emphasized because the intended contribution concerns U.S. financial practice, while international sources were 
included to test convergence and improve transferability. 
The sampling strategy creates clear boundaries. It does not measure the whole scholarly literature, confidential bank practice, or 
criminal prevalence. Authoritative documents may reproduce one another and may privilege institutional perspectives. Those 
limitations are handled through explicit claims: frequency indicates documentary emphasis, not real-world effectiveness. 
3.3 Data Collection and Variables 
Bibliographic fields included document identifier, issuer, title, year, jurisdiction, issuer type, and URL. Eight binary mechanism variables 
were defined before final coding: 
• OW—Accountable ownership: named governance responsibility, executive oversight, defined decision rights, or formal 
accountability. 
• IV—Identity verification: identity proofing, authentication, biometrics, liveness, document validation, or independent 
identity corroboration. 
• DD—Deepfake detection and provenance: synthetic-content detection, watermarking, provenance, authenticity metadata, 
or media forensics. 
• TM—Transaction monitoring: behavioral analytics, device intelligence, payment anomaly detection, holds, or risk-based 
transaction review. 
• HA—Human authentication and escalation: call-back procedures, challenge protocols, dual authorization, employee 
escalation, or authority to pause. 
• CI—Customer information and trust: warnings, consumer education, understandable communication, complaint access, 
inclusion, or trust restoration. 
• IR—Incident response and information sharing: case reporting, suspicious activity reporting, recovery, law-enforcement 
referral, threat intelligence, or post-incident learning. 
• TP—Third-party and platform governance: vendor controls, cloud/model dependencies, telecommunications or platform 
coordination, contractual assurance, or supply-chain risk. 
A code was assigned 1 only where the document contained a substantive recommendation, control, risk discussion, or implementation 
expectation. Passing mention was coded 0. Coding was conservative to reduce interpretive inflation. A document could receive 
multiple codes because layered controls are not mutually exclusive. 
Public trend data were transcribed from annual IC3 reports. The measures are complaint counts, reported dollar losses, loss per 
complaint, year-over-year loss growth, and compound annual growth. The series is contextual rather than a deepfake-specific 
outcome. Dollar values are nominal. No imputation was used. 
3.4 Data Analysis 
For mechanism j across N documents, prevalence was calculated as: 
Prevalence(j) = Σ code(ij) / N × 100. 
Thereafter, the pairwise co-occurrence was examined to identify control bundles. A co-occurrence means only that two mechanisms 
appear in the same document; it does not prove complementarity or effectiveness. Temporal comparisons separated 2019–2022 and

Framework Be Applied in the United States of America? 
JEFMS, Volume 09 Issue 09 September 2026                                       www.ijefm.co.in                                                Page 5003 
2023–2025 sources to explore changes after rapid generative-AI diffusion. Because the sample is purposive and small, no null-
hypothesis significance tests were applied. Inferential p values would imply a probability sample that does not exist. 
For the IC3 series, annual loss growth was calculated as  
(Loss_t / Loss_t−1 − 1) × 100.  
Compound annual growth from 2021 through 2024 was calculated as  
(Loss_2024 / Loss_2021)^(1/3) − 1.  
Ratios were rounded after calculation. These transformations are descriptive. 
Theory development used pattern matching. Codes were mapped to four VTR functions: interruption (IV, DD, TM, HA), calibration (CI 
and explainable verification), recovery (IR), and adaptation (OW, IR, TP). Negative-case analysis examined documents that discussed 
advanced detection without consumer recovery, or customer awareness without operational controls. These cases prevented the 
synthesis from equating any single mechanism with resilience. 
3.5 Validity, Reliability, and Research Integrity 
Construct validity was supported by operational definitions and a binary coding rule. Source triangulation covered law enforcement, 
regulation, standards, and international coordination. An audit trail is provided in Appendix A and the accompanying CSV. Quantitative 
calculations can be reproduced from Table 1. 
Reliability is constrained by single-author coding. To reduce drift, coding was conducted in two passes separated by a full review of 
definitions. Ambiguous cases were resolved toward 0. A future study should use at least two independent coders, report Cohen’s 
kappa or Krippendorff’s alpha, and publish passage-level evidence. The current matrix should be treated as a transparent, revisable 
research instrument. 
Internal validity is limited because document prevalence cannot demonstrate that mechanisms reduce losses or increase trust. The 
paper uses terms such as “supports,” “is consistent with,” and “plausibly contributes” rather than causal language. External validity is 
bounded by English-language public sources and institutional contexts. Public statistics understate unreported events and may include 
changing reporting practices. 
Research integrity required a strict non-fabrication rule. No interviews, survey participants, bank-level incidents, or effect sizes were 
invented. Aggregate fraud figures are not relabeled as deepfake losses. The article is an original synthesis, but no author or software 
can promise a particular similarity-check percentage because databases and algorithms vary. Proper attribution, quotation avoidance, 
and independent phrasing were used throughout.
